claim: The subesophageal zone (SEZ) is a brain region that receives gustatory, pheromonal, and mechanosensory inputs.
source: In insects, the subesophageal zone (SEZ) is a brain region that receives gustatory, pheromonal, and mechanosensory inputs and contributes to the control of diverse behaviors, including feeding, grooming, and locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Ling et al., 2014; Thistle et al., 2012; Thorne et al., 2004; Toda et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004; Weiss et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: The SEZ contributes to the control of diverse behaviors, including feeding, grooming, and locomotion.
source: In insects, the subesophageal zone (SEZ) is a brain region that receives gustatory, pheromonal, and mechanosensory inputs and contributes to the control of diverse behaviors, including feeding, grooming, and locomotion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Bidaye et al., 2020; Flood et al., 2013; Gordon and Scott, 2009; Hampel et al., 2017; Hampel et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Marella et al., 2006; Tastekin et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2004) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: This study generates a collection of split-GAL4 lines that provides precise genetic targeting of 138 different SEZ cell types in adult Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Here, we generate a collection of split-GAL4 lines that provides precise genetic targeting of 138 different SEZ cell types in adult Drosophila melanogaster, comprising approximately one third of all SEZ neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript, including the description of the split-GAL4 collection and the characterization of cell types.

claim: The SEZ Split-GAL4 Collection comprises approximately one third of all SEZ neurons.
source: Here, we generate a collection of split-GAL4 lines that provides precise genetic targeting of 138 different SEZ cell types in adult Drosophila melanogaster, comprising approximately one third of all SEZ neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cell counting data and calculations presented in the Results section.

claim: SEZ neurons cluster by morphology into six supergroups that organize the SEZ into discrete anatomical domains.
source: We characterize the single-cell anatomy of these neurons and find that they cluster by morphology into six supergroups that organize the SEZ into discrete anatomical domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by the NBLAST clustering analysis and morphological data presented in Figure 3 and related results.

claim: The majority of local SEZ interneurons are not classically polarized.
source: We find that the majority of local SEZ interneurons are not classically polarized, suggesting rich local processing, whereas SEZ projection neurons tend to be classically polarized, conveying information to a limited number of higher brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data presented in Figure 10 and the Results section on polarity.

claim: SEZ projection neurons tend to be classically polarized.
source: We find that the majority of local SEZ interneurons are not classically polarized, suggesting rich local processing, whereas SEZ projection neurons tend to be classically polarized, conveying information to a limited number of higher brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data presented in Figure 10 and the Results section on polarity.

claim: The SEZ contains four neuropil subregions: the gnathal ganglia (GNG), saddle (SAD), prow (PRW), and antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC).
source: The SEZ contains four neuropil subregions: the gnathal ganglia (GNG), saddle (SAD), prow (PRW), and antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC; Figure 1A and B; Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ito et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The SEZ contains approximately 1700 neurons.
source: We averaged the estimates based on Dfd and Scr counts to establish a final SEZ cell number estimate of ~1800 cells, of which ~ 1700 are neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cell counting experiments and calculations presented in the Results section 'The SEZ contains about 1700 neurons'.

claim: Dfd-LexA labeled an average of 551 ± 54 cells (n = 7) in the central brain.
source: Dfd-LexA labeled an average of 551 ± 54 cells (n = 7) while Scr-LexA labeled an average of 1115 ± 94 cells (n = 6) in the central brain (Figure 1F), generally consistent with the proportions seen in the transcriptome atlas.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct cell counting data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Scr-LexA labeled an average of 1115 ± 94 cells (n = 6) in the central brain.
source: Dfd-LexA labeled an average of 551 ± 54 cells (n = 7) while Scr-LexA labeled an average of 1115 ± 94 cells (n = 6) in the central brain (Figure 1F), generally consistent with the proportions seen in the transcriptome atlas.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct cell counting data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 277 split-GAL4 lines were generated that provide precise access to single-cell types in the SEZ.
source: We screened ~3400 split-GAL4 combinations using this strategy, which yielded 277 lines that provide precise access to single-cell types in the SEZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the split-GAL4 generation process and the resulting collection.

claim: The 277 split-GAL4 lines label 138 SEZ cell types.
source: These split-GAL4 lines label 138 SEZ cell types, 129 of which have not been previously reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by the characterization of the split-GAL4 collection.

claim: 129 of the 138 SEZ cell types labeled by the split-GAL4 lines have not been previously reported.
source: These split-GAL4 lines label 138 SEZ cell types, 129 of which have not been previously reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previously published literature.

claim: 63 split-GAL4 lines are ideal quality.
source: Amongst the 277 split-GAL4 lines that were generated, 63 are ideal, 86 are excellent, 99 are good, and 29 are poor (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality assessment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 86 split-GAL4 lines are excellent quality.
source: Amongst the 277 split-GAL4 lines that were generated, 63 are ideal, 86 are excellent, 99 are good, and 29 are poor (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality assessment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 99 split-GAL4 lines are good quality.
source: Amongst the 277 split-GAL4 lines that were generated, 63 are ideal, 86 are excellent, 99 are good, and 29 are poor (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality assessment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 29 split-GAL4 lines are poor quality.
source: Amongst the 277 split-GAL4 lines that were generated, 63 are ideal, 86 are excellent, 99 are good, and 29 are poor (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality assessment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The SEZ Split-GAL4 Collection labels 510 neurons out of 1700 estimated SEZ neurons.
source: Taking this into consideration, the collection labels 510 neurons out of 1700 estimated, arguing that the SEZ Split-GAL4 Collection provides approximately 30% coverage of all SEZ neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by counting the number of cell bodies covered by the collection and comparing to the estimated total.

claim: The SEZ Split-GAL4 Collection provides approximately 30% coverage of all SEZ neurons.
source: Taking this into consideration, the collection labels 510 neurons out of 1700 estimated, arguing that the SEZ Split-GAL4 Collection provides approximately 30% coverage of all SEZ neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the calculation based on the number of neurons labeled by the collection divided by the estimated total.

claim: Together, the SEZ Split-GAL4 Collection, the proboscis motor neuron split-GAL4s, and the DN Collection provide precise access to 46% of SEZ neurons (788/1700).
source: Together, the SEZ Split-GAL4 Collection, the proboscis motor neuron split-GAL4s, and the DN Collection provide precise access to 46% of SEZ neurons (788/1700).
evidence: This claim is supported by combining the coverage of multiple split-GAL4 collections.

claim: 121 of the 138 SEZ cell types targeted by the collection are represented in the NBLAST clustering dataset.
source: In total, 121 of the 138 SEZ cell types targeted by the collection are represented in this dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the NBLAST analysis methods.

claim: Six groups were chosen for NBLAST clustering due to the low joining cost and the increase in the differential of Ward's joining cost when moving from six to five groups.
source: We chose six groups due to the low joining cost and the increase in the differential of Ward's joining cost when moving from six to five groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of Ward's joining cost shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The six supergroups are layered from anterior to posterior: groups 1 and 2 most anterior, followed by 3, 5, and finally 6 most posterior.
source: Five of the six supergroups are layered from anterior to posterior: 1 and 2 most anterior, followed by 3, 5, and finally 6 most posterior.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological analysis and visualization of the supergroups in Figure 3B.

claim: Groups 1 and 2 are in a similar anterior plane but group 1 is positioned superior to group 2.
source: Groups 1 and 2 are in a similar anterior plane but group 1 is positioned superior to group 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological analysis and visualization of the supergroups in Figure 3B.

claim: Group 4 sits below the other domains, wrapping the inferior surface of the SEZ.
source: Group 4 sits below these domains, wrapping the inferior surface of the SEZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological analysis and visualization of the supergroups in Figure 3B.

claim: Group 5 appears to form a 'roll' shape and is surrounded by group 3 anterior, group 4 inferior, and group 6 posterior.
source: A lateral view illustrates that group 5 appears to form a 'roll' shape and is surrounded by group 3 anterior, group 4 inferior, and group 6 posterior.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological analysis and visualization of the supergroups in Figure 3B.

claim: Group 1 is composed of 19 cell types that arborize in the prow and flange.
source: Group 1 is composed of neurons that arborize in the prow and flange (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the superior, anterior, and medial regions of the SEZ. Based on their anatomical position, the 19 cell types that make up group 1 may originate from the tritocerebral neuromere.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 4.

claim: Group 1 is neatly split into interneurons and projection neurons.
source: Group 1 is neatly split into interneurons (peep, doublescoop, hyacinth, tulip, horseshoe2, clubround, horseshoe, aster, and oink) and projection neurons (gallinule, kelp, pSG1, amulet, eiffel, aDT6, aSG7, cowboy, hydrangea, and trogon).
evidence: This claim is supported by the classification of cell types in group 1.

claim: All projection neurons in group 1 send arbors to the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP).
source: Notably, all projection neurons in group 1 send arbors to the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: Group 1 includes three previously morphologically described fruitless positive (Fru+) neuronal cell types: pSG1, aSG7, and aDT6.
source: This group includes three previously morphologically described fruitless positive (Fru+) neuronal cell types: pSG1, aSG7, and aDT6 (Liu, 2012; Jai et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Liu, 2012; Jai et al., 2010).

claim: Group 2 contains 18 members, including only SEZ interneurons plus one novel sensory neuron type with cell bodies in the proboscis labellum (diatom).
source: Group 2 contains only SEZ interneurons (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) plus one novel sensory neuron type with cell bodies in the proboscis labellum (diatom; Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Cell types in this group arborize in the anterior and superior region of the GNG, inferior to group 1. Of the 18 members of this group, only one cell type, 'feeding neuron' (Fdg), has been previously described (Flood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 5 and related supplements.

claim: Fdg neurons respond to food presentation in starved flies and activation of Fdg induces a feeding sequence.
source: Fdg neurons respond to food presentation in starved flies and activation of Fdg induces a feeding sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Flood et al., 2013).

claim: Group 3 contains 27 members composed of SEZ projection neurons and interneurons.
source: Group 3 contains 27 members and is composed of SEZ projection neurons and interneurons that overlap with the dendrites of these projection neurons (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 6.

claim: Group 3 projection neurons innervate diverse brain regions, including the superior lateral protocerebrum, superior clamp, and posteriorlateral protocerebrum.
source: In contrast to group 1 projection neurons, group 2 projection neurons innervate diverse brain regions, including the superior lateral protocerebrum, superior clamp, and posteriorlateral protocerebrum, among others.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10. Note: The text says 'group 2 projection neurons' but this appears to be a typo referring to group 3 based on context.

claim: One member of group 3, gustatory second-order neuron type 1 (G2N-1), has been previously reported.
source: One member of group 3 has been previously reported, gustatory second-order neuron type 1 (G2N-1) (Miyazaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Miyazaki et al., 2015).

claim: Group 4 contains 26 members including interneurons that arborize in the inferior GNG and wrap the inferior surface of the GNG.
source: Group 4 contains interneurons that arborize in the inferior GNG and wrap the inferior surface of the GNG (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1). Group 4 sits inferior to groups 2 and 3. Notably, group 4 includes six novel DNs that arborize in the GNG and frequently descend to the leg neuropil (LegNp) in the prothoracic neuromere (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; Court et al., 2020). Of the 26 members of group 4, only one, tyrosine hydroxylase ventral unpaired medial (TH-VUM), has been previously reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 7.

claim: Group 4 includes six novel DNs that arborize in the GNG and frequently descend to the leg neuropil (LegNp) in the prothoracic neuromere.
source: Notably, group 4 includes six novel DNs that arborize in the GNG and frequently descend to the leg neuropil (LegNp) in the prothoracic neuromere (Figure 7—figure supplement 2; Court et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: TH-VUM is a dopaminergic neuron that influences the probability of proboscis extension.
source: TH-VUM is a dopaminergic neuron that influences the probability of proboscis extension (Marella et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Marella et al., 2012).

claim: Group 5 contains 27 interneurons, projection neurons, and DNs that arborize just posterior to the boundary between the anterior and posterior SEZ.
source: Group 5 contains 27 interneurons, projection neurons, and DNs that arborize just posterior to the boundary between the anterior and posterior SEZ, flanked by groups 3, 4, and 6 on the anterior, inferior, and posterior sides, respectively (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 8.

claim: Projection neurons in group 5 arborize in the lobula, inferior and superior clamp, and inferior bridge, among other regions.
source: Projection neurons in group 5 arborize in the lobula, inferior and superior clamp, and inferior bridge, among other regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: The seven DNs in group 5 send their axons most frequently to the leg neuropils and to the abdominal ganglion (Abd).
source: The seven DNs in this group send their axons most frequently to the leg neuropils and to the abdominal ganglion (Abd; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Three members of group 5 have been previously reported: aSG1, aSG4, and aDN1.
source: Three members of group 5 have been previously reported. Two are previously described Fru+ neurons, aSG1 and aSG4 (Jai et al., 2010). The third neuronal type, aDN1, triggers antennal grooming when activated (Hampel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Jai et al., 2010; Hampel et al., 2015).

claim: aDN1 triggers antennal grooming when activated.
source: The third neuronal type, aDN1, triggers antennal grooming when activated (Hampel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Hampel et al., 2015).

claim: Group 6 contains nine members including neurons in the posterior of the brain, spanning the GNG, inferior posterior slope, and superior posterior slope.
source: Group 6 contains neurons in the posterior of the brain, spanning the GNG, inferior posterior slope, and superior posterior slope (Figure 9 and Figure 9—figure supplement 1) and is the most posterior group in the SEZ. This small group contains only nine members, and group 6 cell types do not project to higher neuropils.
evidence: This claim is supported by the morphological characterization shown in Figure 9.

claim: Group 6 cell types do not project to higher neuropils.
source: This small group contains only nine members, and group 6 cell types do not project to higher neuropils.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: One member of group 6, dubbed knees, is a DN that innervates neck neuropil and wing neuropil.
source: One member, dubbed knees, is a DN that innervates neck neuropil and wing neuropil.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: No members of group 6 have been previously reported.
source: No members of this morphological group have been previously reported.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previously published literature.

claim: The 121 cell types analyzed for polarity include 81 interneuron cell types, 26 projection neuron cell types, 13 DN cell types, and 1 sensory neuron cell type.
source: These 121 cell types include 81 interneuron cell types, 26 projection neuron cell types, 13 DN cell types, and 1 sensory neuron cell type.
evidence: This claim is supported by the classification of cell types for polarity analysis.

claim: Among the SEZ interneuron cell types analyzed, 39/81 (48%) have mixed polarity.
source: Among the SEZ interneuron cell types we analyzed, 39/81 (48%) have mixed polarity, 22/81 (27%) have biased polarity, and 20/81 (25%) are classically polarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Among the SEZ interneuron cell types analyzed, 22/81 (27%) have biased polarity.
source: Among the SEZ interneuron cell types we analyzed, 39/81 (48%) have mixed polarity, 22/81 (27%) have biased polarity, and 20/81 (25%) are classically polarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Among the SEZ interneuron cell types analyzed, 20/81 (25%) are classically polarized.
source: Among the SEZ interneuron cell types we analyzed, 39/81 (48%) have mixed polarity, 22/81 (27%) have biased polarity, and 20/81 (25%) are classically polarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: All group 2 interneurons (making up 17/18 cell types in group 2) have either biased or mixed polarity.
source: However, all group 2 interneurons (making up 17/18 cell types in group 2) have either biased or mixed polarity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: Most SEZ projection neurons analyzed in this study are clearly polarized (20/26, 77%).
source: Most SEZ projection neurons analyzed in this study are clearly polarized (20/26, 77%). However, a few have biased (4/26, 15%) or mixed polarity (2/26, 8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: 4/26 (15%) of SEZ projection neurons have biased polarity.
source: Most SEZ projection neurons analyzed in this study are clearly polarized (20/26, 77%). However, a few have biased (4/26, 15%) or mixed polarity (2/26, 8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: 2/26 (8%) of SEZ projection neurons have mixed polarity.
source: Most SEZ projection neurons analyzed in this study are clearly polarized (20/26, 77%). However, a few have biased (4/26, 15%) or mixed polarity (2/26, 8%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: All projection neuron cell types with biased polarity have axons in the SMP and belong to group 1.
source: In contrast, all projection neuron cell types with biased polarity have axons in the SMP and belong to group 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: No projection neurons were identified that link the SEZ directly to the central complex or the mushroom body.
source: We did not identify any projection neurons that link the SEZ directly to the central complex or the mushroom body.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: 5/13 (39%) of the novel SEZ DNs have biased polarity.
source: Analyzing the polarity of the novel SEZ DNs described here, we find that 5/13 (39%) have biased polarity, 2/13 (15%) have mixed polarity, and 6/13 (46%) are clearly polarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: 2/13 (15%) of the novel SEZ DNs have mixed polarity.
source: Analyzing the polarity of the novel SEZ DNs described here, we find that 5/13 (39%) have biased polarity, 2/13 (15%) have mixed polarity, and 6/13 (46%) are clearly polarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: 6/13 (46%) of the novel SEZ DNs are clearly polarized.
source: Analyzing the polarity of the novel SEZ DNs described here, we find that 5/13 (39%) have biased polarity, 2/13 (15%) have mixed polarity, and 6/13 (46%) are clearly polarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity analysis data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The novel SEZ DNs have outputs in the neck, haltere, and leg neuropils (in all three neuromeres), and in the abdominal ganglion.
source: These DNs have outputs in the neck, haltere, and leg neuropils (in all three neuromeres), and in the abdominal ganglion, consistent with the observation that GNG DNs are frequently connected with the leg neuropils (Namiki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: GNG DNs are frequently connected with the leg neuropils.
source: These DNs have outputs in the neck, haltere, and leg neuropils (in all three neuromeres), and in the abdominal ganglion, consistent with the observation that GNG DNs are frequently connected with the leg neuropils (Namiki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Namiki et al., 2018).

claim: 149/277 split-GAL4 lines are classified as ideal or excellent.
source: Most of the SEZ Split-GAL4 lines are specific, with 149/277 lines classified as ideal or excellent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality assessment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The SEZ is situated in a central location between the motor circuits of the ventral nerve cord (VNC) and the higher order brain regions of the supraesophageal zone.
source: Defined as the brain tissue below the esophageal foramen, it is situated in a central location between the motor circuits of the ventral nerve cord (VNC) and the higher order brain regions of the supraesophageal zone (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Ito et al., 2014).

claim: The SEZ participates in many context-dependent motor actions, including feeding, grooming, and locomotion.
source: In Drosophila and other insects, the SEZ participates in many context-dependent motor actions, including feeding, grooming, and locomotion, with evidence suggesting that it is involved in action selection (Bidaye et al., 2020; Flood et al., 2013; Gordon and Scott, 2009; Hampel et al., 2017; Hampel et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Marella et al., 2006; Tastekin et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Evidence suggests that the SEZ is involved in action selection.
source: In Drosophila and other insects, the SEZ participates in many context-dependent motor actions, including feeding, grooming, and locomotion, with evidence suggesting that it is involved in action selection (Bidaye et al., 2020; Flood et al., 2013; Gordon and Scott, 2009; Hampel et al., 2017; Hampel et al., 2015; Mann et al., 2013; Manzo et al., 2012; Marella et al., 2006; Tastekin et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SEZ receives direct sensory input from axonal arbors of gustatory and mechanosensory peripheral neurons.
source: It receives direct sensory input from axonal arbors of gustatory and mechanosensory peripheral neurons and indirect input from pheromone-sensing neurons (Ling et al., 2014; Thistle et al., 2012; Thorne et al., 2004; Toda et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004; Weiss et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The SEZ receives indirect input from pheromone-sensing neurons.
source: It receives direct sensory input from axonal arbors of gustatory and mechanosensory peripheral neurons and indirect input from pheromone-sensing neurons (Ling et al., 2014; Thistle et al., 2012; Thorne et al., 2004; Toda et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004; Weiss et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Two major outputs of the SEZ are descending neurons that convey information to the VNC and motor neurons that control the movement of the proboscis and antennae.
source: Two major outputs of the SEZ are descending neurons that convey information to the VNC and motor neurons that control the movement of the proboscis and antennae (McKellar et al., 2020; Namiki et al., 2018; Stocker et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent work has delineated fascicle and neuropil-based columnar domains in the SEZ that are identifiable throughout development.
source: Recent work has delineated fascicle and neuropil-based columnar domains in the SEZ that are identifiable throughout development and has mapped sensory substructures in the SEZ in larvae and adults (Hartenstein et al., 2018; Kendroud et al., 2018; Miroschnikow et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent work has mapped sensory substructures in the SEZ in larvae and adults.
source: Recent work has delineated fascicle and neuropil-based columnar domains in the SEZ that are identifiable throughout development and has mapped sensory substructures in the SEZ in larvae and adults (Hartenstein et al., 2018; Kendroud et al., 2018; Miroschnikow et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Recent electron microscopy datasets provide unprecedented synaptic resolution of approximately 100,000 neurons that comprise the adult D. melanogaster brain.
source: Recent electron microscopy datasets provide unprecedented synaptic resolution of approximately 100,000 neurons that comprise the adult D. melanogaster brain (Scheffer et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The split-GAL4 method uses two different enhancers to independently drive expression of either the GAL4 transcriptional activation domain (AD) or DNA-binding domain (DBD).
source: In this intersectional method, two different enhancers are used to independently drive expression of either the GAL4 transcriptional activation domain (AD) or DNA-binding domain (DBD).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of the split-GAL4 method.

claim: The GAL4 AD and DBD domains heterodimerize through leucine zipper fragments and drive transgene expression restricted to the intersection of the two expression patterns.
source: These domains heterodimerize through leucine zipper fragments and drive transgene expression restricted to the intersection of the two expression patterns (Luan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Luan et al., 2006).

claim: Of the 56,902 high-quality cells represented in the single-cell transcriptome atlas, 390 are Dfd-positive, 691 are Scr-positive, 134 are lab-positive, and 15 express both Dfd and lab.
source: Of the 56,902 high-quality cells represented in the atlas, 390 are Dfd-positive, 691 are Scr-positive, 134 are lab-positive, and 15 express both Dfd and lab (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the single-cell transcriptome atlas data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 1182/1230 (96.1%) of cells expressing SEZ neuromere-specific markers are assigned to neuronal clusters based upon expression of neuronal genes.
source: Together, 1230 cells in the atlas express these neuromere-specific markers, with 1182/1230 (96.1%) assigned to neuronal clusters based upon expression of neuronal genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the single-cell transcriptome atlas data.

claim: Previous estimates of secondary SEZ neuron number based on neuroblasts predicted ~2000 SEZ neurons.
source: These estimates are roughly consistent with previous estimates of secondary SEZ neuron number based on neuroblasts, which predicted ~2000 SEZ neurons (Kuert et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Kuert et al., 2014).

claim: Some deutocerebral commissures cross below the esophageal foramen.
source: However, previous reports demonstrate that some deutocerebral commissures cross below the esophageal foramen, and therefore an unknown number of deutocerebral cell bodies may be part of the SEZ (Boyan et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research (Boyan et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2014).

claim: An unknown number of deutocerebral cell bodies may be part of the SEZ.
source: However, previous reports demonstrate that some deutocerebral commissures cross below the esophageal foramen, and therefore an unknown number of deutocerebral cell bodies may be part of the SEZ (Boyan et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from previous research showing deutocerebral commissures crossing below the esophageal foramen.

claim: The estimate of SEZ cell number is likely an underestimate.
source: Thus, our estimate of SEZ cell number is likely an underestimate.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the limitations of the counting method.

claim: Recent work has established reliable anatomical criteria that define the boundaries between the four SEZ neuromeres and has mapped all secondary lineages of the SEZ.
source: However, recent work has established reliable anatomical criteria that define the boundaries between the four SEZ neuromeres and has mapped all secondary lineages of the SEZ (Hartenstein et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Hartenstein et al., 2018).

claim: Approximately 3400 split-GAL4 combinations were screened.
source: We screened ~3400 split-GAL4 combinations using this strategy, which yielded 277 lines that provide precise access to single-cell types in the SEZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the screening process.

claim: 17 split-GAL4 lines specifically target SEZ motor neurons of the proboscis, totaling 36 cell bodies.
source: In addition, 17 split-GAL4 lines specifically target SEZ motor neurons of the proboscis, totaling 36 cell bodies (McKellar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (McKellar et al., 2020).

claim: The descending interneuron (DN) Split-GAL4 Collection contains 41 DN cell types that comprise 242 additional cell bodies in the SEZ (out of 360 total DN cell bodies in the SEZ).

claim: The mixed polarity of SEZ interneurons argues for local and reciprocal connectivity between neurons, with information flowing in networks rather than unidirectional streams.
source: The mixed polarity of the SEZ interneurons argues for local and reciprocal connectivity between neurons, with information flowing in networks rather than unidirectional streams.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the polarity analysis data.

claim: Projection neurons may serve chiefly to pass information from highly interconnected SEZ circuits to other brain regions in a unidirectional manner.
source: Projection neurons, in contrast, may serve chiefly to pass information from highly interconnected SEZ circuits to other brain regions in a unidirectional manner.

claim: Many SEZ projection neurons innervate the SMP—a region known to contain neurosecretory cell types.
source: Notably, we identified many SEZ projection neurons that innervate the SMP—a region known to contain neurosecretory cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polarity and innervation analysis data and established knowledge about the SMP.

claim: The frequent innervation of the SMP by SEZ projection neurons may betray a role for acute taste detection or feeding circuit activation in the regulation of hormone secretion.
source: This may betray a role for acute taste detection or feeding circuit activation in the regulation of hormone secretion.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the innervation patterns.

claim: The frequent innervation of the superior lateral protocerebrum and lateral horn by SEZ projection neurons may hint at the site of olfactory-gustatory synthesis.
source: In addition, the frequent innervation of the superior lateral protocerebrum and lateral horn by SEZ projection neurons may hint at the site of olfactory-gustatory synthesis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the innervation patterns.

claim: Taste information influences local search behaviors during foraging, a task that is expected to involve the central complex.
source: As an example, taste information influences local search behaviors during foraging, a task that is expected to involve the central complex (Haberkern et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Haberkern et al., 2019).

claim: The mushroom body is known to respond to taste.
source: Furthermore, the mushroom body is known to respond to taste, raising the possibility that taste information from gustatory sensory neuron axons in the SEZ must be relayed through yet another brain region before reaching mushroom body cell types (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Harris et al., 2015).

claim: Taste information from gustatory sensory neuron axons in the SEZ may be relayed through another brain region before reaching mushroom body cell types.
source: Furthermore, the mushroom body is known to respond to taste, raising the possibility that taste information from gustatory sensory neuron axons in the SEZ must be relayed through yet another brain region before reaching mushroom body cell types (Harris et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the lack of direct connectivity and known mushroom body responses to taste.

claim: Group 1 neurons may impinge on neurosecretory neurons or function in energy and fluid homeostasis circuits.
source: Based on anatomical position and the known function of a few SEZ neurons, it is tempting to speculate that different morphological clusters may participate in different behavioral functions. Group 1 contains projection neurons that innervate the region of the SMP surrounding the pars intercerebralis (PI), suggesting that group 1 neurons may impinge on neurosecretory neurons or function in energy and fluid homeostasis circuits.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from anatomical position and innervation patterns.

claim: The proximity of group 1 interneurons to previously described interoceptive SEZ neurons (ISNs) and ingestion neurons (IN1) supports the hypothesis that group 1 neurons function in energy and fluid homeostasis circuits.
source: The proximity of group 1 interneurons to previously described interoceptive SEZ neurons (ISNs) (Jourjine et al., 2016) and ingestion neurons (IN1) (Yapici et al., 2016) supports this hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from anatomical proximity and citations to previous research.

claim: Group 2 neurons may have roles in feeding sequence generation.
source: Group 2 contains Fdg, a feeding-related neuron, as well as cell types (indigo, tinctoria) that are located near pumping motor neurons (Manzo et al., 2012; McKellar et al., 2020), suggesting that group 2 neurons have roles in feeding sequence generation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the presence of Fdg and proximity to pumping motor neurons.

claim: Group 3 may, in part, be composed of taste-responsive neurons.
source: Group 3 contains G2N-1, a candidate second-order gustatory neuron, and projection neurons that innervate recently described taste-responsive SLP regions (Kim et al., 2017; Snell et al., 2020), suggesting that group 3 may, in part, be composed of taste-responsive neurons.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the presence of G2N-1 and innervation of taste-responsive regions.

claim: Group 4 members may function in proboscis motor control.
source: Many interneurons in group 4 are located near proboscis motor neurons that control rostrum protraction, haustellum extension, and labellar spreading (Kendroud et al., 2018; McKellar et al., 2020), indicating that group 4 members function in proboscis motor control.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from proximity to proboscis motor neurons.

claim: Group 5 neurons may participate in circuits that control grooming and stopping behaviors.
source: The proximity of neurons in group 5 to previously described stopping neuron MAN (Bidaye et al., 2014), and the inclusion of an antennal grooming neuron, suggests that group 5 neurons may participate in circuits that control grooming and stopping behaviors.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from proximity to MAN and the presence of an antennal grooming neuron.

claim: Group 6 is located in the posterior SEZ and posterior slope, regions implicated in flight behaviors, including wing and neck control.
source: Group 6 is located in the posterior SEZ and posterior slope, regions implicated in flight behaviors, including wing and neck control (Namiki et al., 2018; Robie et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The roles of the neurons described here are likely more diverse than the hypothesized behavioral functions for each supergroup.
source: While we hypothesize potential behavioral functions for each supergroup, we readily acknowledge that the roles of the neurons described here are likely more diverse.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: The study identified 91 local interneurons, 30 projection neurons, 16 descending neurons, and 1 sensory neuron.
source: We identified 91 local interneurons, 30 projection neurons, 16 descending neurons, and 1 sensory neuron.
evidence: This claim is supported by the classification of cell types in the collection.

claim: Polarity analyses of the lateral horn, mushroom body, descending neurons, and protocerebral bridge identified few neurons with completely mixed polarity.
source: Polarity analyses of the lateral horn, mushroom body, descending neurons, and protocerebral bridge identified few neurons with completely mixed polarity (Aso et al., 2014a; Aso et al., 2014b; Dolan et al., 2019; Namiki et al., 2018; Wolff and Rubin, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research (Pfeiffer and Homberg, 2014).
